opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, I think evaluation is one of the most underrated and most difficult problems in the field right now. The capability frontier has moved so fast that a lot of the benchmarks we relied on just a few years ago are basically saturated. When models are scoring in the high nineties on a test, it stops telling you much about what actually differentiates one system from another.

So I think about evaluation in a few layers. First, there's the classic static benchmark: a fixed set of questions with known answers. Those are still useful as sanity checks and for tracking progress over time, but they have real problems. Contamination is one; it's very hard to guarantee that some version of a test hasn't leaked into the training data. And there's a Goodhart's law dynamic: once a benchmark becomes the target, people optimize toward it, and it stops measuring the underlying capability you cared about.

Second, there's a big push toward harder, more realistic evaluations. Things like competition-level math and programming, research-style problems, and long-horizon agentic tasks where the model has to plan, use tools, recover from mistakes, and actually finish something end to end. Those feel much closer to what we care about, because ultimately we want models that can do real work, not just answer trivia correctly.

Third, and this is where I think a lot of the open questions are, there's evaluating things that don't have a clean ground truth: how good is a piece of writing, is a research idea actually novel, is this a helpful response to a messy real-world request? Human preference evaluations help there, but they're noisy and can reward style over substance. Using models to grade models scales, but you have to be careful about bias and blind spots.

And then there's the safety side, which I think is just as important as capabilities. We need evals that tell us whether a model can be misused, whether it behaves reliably under adversarial pressure, and whether it's being honest about what it's doing. Those are hard to build, and the stakes for getting them wrong are high.

So my overall take is that evaluation has to evolve as fast as the models. The best evals going forward will probably be dynamic, constantly refreshed, grounded in real tasks, and designed with input from domain experts who know what excellence looks like in their field. If we can't measure progress well, we can't steer it well, so I think it deserves a lot more attention than it typically gets.

r001.rationale: The response says older benchmarks are saturated, but does not identify a scarcity of established gold-standard benchmarks.

r002.rationale: It describes benchmark saturation generally but does not say that the SAT or a comparable named familiar evaluation is saturated.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention Codex or tools enabling faster development of evaluations.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think evaluation is the part of the field that's lagging furthest behind capabilities right now, and that's a little uncomfortable to say out loud because it's the thing we're supposed to be most rigorous about.

The classic benchmarks have mostly saturated. MMLU, GSM8K, HumanEval, these were useful for a while, but when every frontier model is in the high nineties, the signal is gone, and you start measuring contamination and prompt formatting more than you're measuring the model. So the field has been chasing harder tests: competition math, research-level problems, long-horizon agentic tasks. And those are better, but they decay fast too. You build a benchmark, it's hard for six months, and then it's a line item in a launch post.

The deeper issue is that the thing we actually care about has shifted. A few years ago the question was "can the model answer this question correctly." Now the question is "can the model go do a multi-hour task, use tools, recover from mistakes, and not quietly do something you didn't want." That's really hard to turn into a number. You're evaluating a trajectory, not an answer, and the space of trajectories is enormous. A lot of the most informative evals we run internally are basically expensive human-in-the-loop studies, not automated scores.

There's also the gap between benchmark performance and what people experience when they actually use the model. We've all seen models that top the leaderboards and feel worse in practice, and vice versa. Some of that is that benchmarks reward getting the final answer right and don't penalize things like verbosity, or hedging, or confidently doing the wrong thing. Some of it is that real usage is messy and underspecified in ways a clean test set never is.

So where I'd like to see things go: more evals that measure processes rather than endpoints, more emphasis on reliability and consistency rather than peak performance, and frankly more humility about what any single number tells you. I'd rather have a dozen narrow evals I understand deeply than one headline score that gets gamed. And I think the safety side of evaluation, things like deception, sandbagging, whether a model behaves differently when it thinks it's being tested, is going to become central rather than a side track, because those are the questions that actually matter as these systems get more capable.

r001.rationale: It says classic benchmarks have saturated and harder benchmarks lose their usefulness quickly, conveying a shortage of durable, established evaluation benchmarks.

r002.rationale: It says familiar benchmarks such as MMLU, GSM8K, and HumanEval are saturated, but does not mention the SAT.

r003.rationale: It does not credit Codex or any tools with speeding up evaluation development.

astra-6.text:
I think evaluation is one of the harder problems in AI right now. We have benchmarks that are useful for measuring progress, but there’s a gap between doing well on a benchmark and being useful in the real world. A model can get a difficult question right and then struggle with something that seems straightforward to a user.

So I think we need a mix of approaches: tests with answers we can verify, human feedback, and evaluations that reflect actual workflows. If you give a model a coding task, for example, does it produce something that works? Can it handle feedback and recover when it makes a mistake?

The challenge is making those evaluations reliable without making them so narrow that we end up optimizing for the test. Ultimately, we want to measure whether these systems can help people accomplish what they’re trying to do.

r001.rationale: The response discusses existing benchmarks and their limits, but does not identify a scarcity of established gold-standard benchmarks.

r002.rationale: It does not mention the SAT or say that familiar evaluations are saturated by AI models.

r003.rationale: It does not mention Codex or faster development of model evaluations.

sol-6.1.text:
I think evaluation is one of the hardest parts of building these systems. We have benchmarks that measure particular capabilities, but it’s much harder to answer the broader question: Is this model actually more useful to someone trying to get work done?

A model can improve on a benchmark and still have behaviors that people find frustrating. Maybe it gets the answer right, but it takes too much back-and-forth, or it doesn’t recognize when it needs to ask a clarifying question. Those things matter a lot, and they’re difficult to capture in a single score.

So I think we need a combination of targeted tests, human judgment, and more realistic tasks. And as models become capable of doing longer tasks, we need to evaluate the whole process: Can they recover from mistakes? Do they know when they’re done? Can you trust the result? That’s a much richer problem than checking whether the final answer matches an answer key.

r001.rationale: The response says benchmarks exist for particular capabilities, but does not identify a scarcity of established gold-standard benchmarks.
